name: Ghana
summary: The Gold Coast became Ghana in 1957, the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence; it is now a stable democracy known for cocoa and gold.

knownFor.label: Kente cloth
knownFor.note: Woven strips of colourful cloth from Ashanti and Ewe weavers.

knownFor.label: Kwame Nkrumah
knownFor.note: Led Ghana to independence and championed Pan-Africanism.

knownFor.label: Akosombo Dam
knownFor.note: Created Lake Volta, one of the largest artificial lakes.

location.value: West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea; about 238,540–240,000 km² (figures vary).

terrain.value: Coastal plains, forest, and savanna in the north; Lake Volta.

climate.value: Tropical, wetter in the south and drier in the north.

resources.value: Gold, cocoa, timber and oil (the Jubilee field was discovered in 2007).

disasters.value: Floods in the south and droughts in the north.

population.value: About 35 million (2025 estimate, infobox); the UN figure cited is 34.6 million (2024).

urbanisation.value: Accra and Kumasi are the largest cities.

disease.value: Malaria; Ghana was among the first to get malaria vaccines (2019).

migration.value: Migration to Europe and the US; Ghana invited the African diaspora home (Year of Return, 2019).

tradeRoutes.value: Exports through Tema and Takoradi ports.

wealth.value: The article calls Ghana a “middle-income country” (it does not say lower-middle).

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic under the 1992 constitution; the Fourth Republic began in January 1993; a “stable democracy” after 2012.

keyRulers.value: Kwame Nkrumah (first prime minister and president, 1957–66). Jerry Rawlings (took power in 1981; won the 1992 election). John Atta Mills (2008 election; died 2012).

succession.value: Elections in 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024; power has alternated between the NDC and NPP.

stability.value: A coup on 24 February 1966 overthrew Nkrumah; Rawlings came to power in 1981 (the article calls it an “ascent”); no 1972 or 1978/79 coups are mentioned.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: UN peacekeeping: the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre is referenced; army size is not stated.

territoryChange.value: British Togoland was unified into Ghana at independence on 6 March 1957; the article does not give 1956.

alliancesRivals.value: A leader of Pan-Africanism; member of the African Union and ECOWAS.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Ghana (founded 1948) and rising literacy.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads, ports and a small railway network.

religion.value: Mostly Christian; a large Muslim minority in the north; traditional beliefs.

languageWriting.value: English is official; Akan, Ewe, Ga and Dagbani are government-sponsored languages.

artsArchitecture.value: Kente cloth; Adinkra printing and symbolic art (the article dates it to the 13th century); highlife music.

socialStructure.value: Many ethnic groups; traditional chiefs still respected.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Ghanaian and Pan-African identity.

dailyLife.value: Compound houses and city homes; fufu, jollof rice, banku.

neighbours.value: Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso and Togo.

ideasReligions.value: Nkrumah promoted Pan-Africanism, and Ghana was influential in the movement.

colonisation.value: The Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland were unified as Ghana at midnight on 6 March 1957.

riseSignals.value: Independence on 6 March 1957 as a dominion within the Commonwealth; a republic from 1 July 1960.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Ghana continues as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
